title: Lesson 7: Geometry Speed — Triangle and Area Shortcuts
subtopics: Fill-the-step: area by Heron's for 3-4-5 triangle
Composite figure area by triangle decomposition
Challenge: prove 7-24-25 triple and find area
learningGoals: Identify Pythagorean triples instantly using pattern recognition (3-4-5 family and 5-12-13 family).
Apply the half-base-times-height formula at speed, including fractional heights.
Use Heron's formula mentally for small integer-side triangles.
coreIdeas: Pythagorean triples follow scaling patterns: any multiple of a triple is also a triple (e.g., 6-8-10 from 3-4-5).
Triangle area = ½ × base × height. When height is a fraction, multiply base and height first, then halve — one mental step.
Heron's formula: area = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)) where s = (a+b+c)/2. For small integers, s and the product are easy to compute mentally.

sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise B: Triangle area at speed
sessionFlow.coachHook: Area = ½ × base × height. Speed trick: halve the base first, then multiply by height. Or halve the height first — whichever gives a whole number faster!
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Base 14, height 9: halve base → 7. 7×9=63. Base 15, height 4: halve height → 2. 15×2=30.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 and height 5.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Speed area computed! Choosing which factor to halve first saves mental effort.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Find areas: base 20 height 11, base 9 height 14.

exercises.questionText: Find the area of a triangle with base = 14 cm and height = 9 cm.

For area = ½ × 15 × 8, which factoring gives a whole number immediately?
options: Both give whole numbers; halving 8 first is simpler
exercises.expectedAnswer: Both give whole numbers; halving 8 first is simpler
exercises.hint: Halving 8 gives 4 (whole). Halving 15 gives 7.5. Prefer halving even numbers.

sessionFlow.coachHook: When triangle sides share a pattern — like a scaled triple or an isosceles pair — perimeter is a one-step mental sum!
sessionFlow.boardDemo: Isosceles: sides 13, 13, 10. Perimeter = 2×13+10 = 26+10 = 36. Scaled 3-4-5 with k=6: sides 18, 24, 30. Perimeter = 6×(3+4+5) = 6×12 = 72.

sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Perimeter of isosceles triangle with equal sides 17 cm and base 12 cm.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Perimeter shortcut used! Factoring the scale is faster than adding all three sides.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Find perimeter: 8-15-17 scaled by 3, isosceles with equal sides 25 and base 14.

sessionFlow.subtopic: Composite figure area by triangle decomposition
sessionFlow.missionStepTitle: Exercise G: Composite figures by triangle decomposition
sessionFlow.coachHook: Any polygon can be split into triangles. Find the area of each triangle and add them up. This is the Vedic decompose-then-combine strategy!
sessionFlow.boardDemo: A quadrilateral split by a diagonal into two triangles. Base 10, heights 6 and 4. Total area = ½×10×6 + ½×10×4 = 30+20 = 50.
sessionFlow.readAloudPrompt: A rectangle 8×5. Split it into two equal triangles. Area of each?
sessionFlow.tryPrompt: Parallelogram with base 12 and height 7 — split into two triangles to find area.
sessionFlow.masteryCheck: L-shaped figure: split into two rectangles or three triangles. If given dimensions compute total area.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackWin: Decomposition complete! Splitting into triangles is a universal area strategy.
sessionFlow.instantFeedbackRetry: Parallelogram 12×7: two triangles each = ½×12×7=42. Total=84. Same as base×height.
sessionFlow.reviewPrompt: Find area of a hexagon with all sides 6 by splitting into 6 triangles.

exercises.questionText: A quadrilateral is split by a diagonal into two triangles with the same base 10. Their heights are 6 and 4. Total area = ?
exercises.solution: Triangle 1: ½×10×6=30. Triangle 2: ½×10×4=20. Total: 50 sq units.

exercises.questionText: An L-shaped figure is split into two rectangles: 8×4 and 3×2. Total area = ?
exercises.solution: Rectangle 1: 8×4=32. Rectangle 2: 3×2=6. Total area=38 sq units.

teachingScript.teacherLine: Three seed triples: 3-4-5, 5-12-13, 8-15-17. Multiply all three sides by any positive integer to get a new triple. The Vedic insight: proportionality preserves the right angle.
teachingScript.boardAction: Draw the three seed triples. Show 2×(3-4-5)=6-8-10 by scaling arrows.

teachingScript.teacherLine: Heron's formula: s = half perimeter. Area = √(s(s−a)(s−b)(s−c)). For integer-side triangles the product under the square root is always a perfect square.
teachingScript.boardAction: Show 5-12-13 Heron's calculation with each factor highlighted.

teachingScript.teacherLine: Six boxes, six seconds each. Fill the Heron's template and the answer reveals itself.
teachingScript.boardAction: Show blank 6-box Heron's template for 3-4-5. Walk through one box at a time.

teachingScript.teacherLine: The 7-24-25 triple is lesser known but just as beautiful. Prove it, compute the area two ways, and you have mastered every triangle tool in this lesson.
teachingScript.boardAction: Write 7²+24²=49+576=625=25². Box the proof. Then show area both ways.
teachingScript.microPractice: Prove (20,21,29) is a triple and find its area.
